subject: Economy
theme: Capital flows to developing countries and financial crisis resilience
question_short_text: Which type of capital inflow is most beneficial for host developing countries given crises experience?
text: Global capital flows to developing countries increased significantly during the nineties. In view of the East Asian financial crisis and Latin American experience, which type of inflow is good for the host country?
explanation: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is the best type of inflow because it involves long-term commitments, stability, real productive investment, technology transfer, and job creation, rather than short-term speculative flows that can reverse suddenly during crises.

research.summary: This question tests the critical distinction between stable long-term capital flows and volatile short-term flows—a lesson written in the crises of the 1990s. The East Asian financial crisis (1997–98) and the earlier Latin American debt crisis (1982 onwards) both exposed the dangers of excessive reliance on short-term, debt-based capital flows. In East Asia, the problem was not primarily FDI but rather portfolio investment and short-term bank lending. When confidence evaporated, investors fled en masse, turning "hot money" inflows into devastating capital outflows. The crisis began when Thailand sought to unpeg the baht, but the deeper vulnerability lay in the financial system's dependence on "expensive and highly conditioned short-term capital flow." Once panic set in, the resulting capital flight and credit crunch amplified currency depreciation and banking sector collapse. By contrast, FDI flows during the crisis proved remarkably resilient. Foreign direct investors—those who had built factories, operations, and management structures—did not stampede out. They either maintained or increased operations, sometimes even acquiring distressed assets at lower prices. Data shows that while portfolio equity investment and bank lending turned sharply negative in 1997 for the crisis-hit countries (Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand), FDI flows remained positive, even growing in certain sectors. This resilience explains why Asia recovered more quickly than Latin America did after the debt crisis. Latin America's 1980s crisis illustrates the other extreme: commercial bank loans and portfolio debt had ballooned in the 1970s and early 1980s when petrodollar recycling was easy and rates were low. When the Volcker Shock hit (1979–82) and interest rates soared, Latin American countries faced unsustainable debt service burdens. Unlike FDI investors, commercial lenders stopped new lending and demanded repayment. The sudden cutoff plunged much of the region into the "lost decade." The difference is structural: FDI involves real, productive activity and management stakes that make reversal costly and irrational. FDI brings technology, skills, managerial expertise, infrastructure development, and permanent job creation. A multinational firm that has invested in a factory cannot simply withdraw overnight without massive losses. Portfolio investors, by contrast, own liquid securities that can be sold in minutes at the push of a button. Commercial loans are contractual obligations that can be suddenly recalled. Both are vulnerable to panic and contagion in ways FDI is not. The empirical evidence bears this out: research shows FDI inflows have lower volatility and greater resilience during financial crises compared to portfolio and debt flows. For developing countries, FDI represents confidence in the economy itself—an investor betting real capital on long-term productive returns, not just speculation on currency or stock prices.
facts: FDI volatility is substantially lower than portfolio investment volatility; during the 1997–98 Asian crisis, FDI inflows remained positive while portfolio equity turned sharply negative across crisis-hit countries.
The Latin American debt crisis of 1982 was driven primarily by commercial bank loans and syndicated debt, not FDI; when lending tightened, the region entered a deep recession lasting a decade.

East Asia recovered faster from the 1997–98 crisis than Latin America recovered from the 1980s debt crisis, partly because FDI-dependent economies had a more stable foundation of long-term productive investment.
FDI generates technology transfer, skills development, job creation, and infrastructure investment—direct spillovers to the host economy that portfolio investment and commercial loans do not provide.

External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) and commercial loans expose countries to interest rate risk and sudden withdrawal, as evidenced by the tightening of lending after the 1981–82 Volcker Shock raised global interest rates.
